rules.title: JavaScript interface exposed without URL allowlist
rules.description: The WebView adds a JavaScript interface that exposes native methods, but navigation is not restricted to trusted origins. A remote attacker can redirect the WebView and call the interface.
rules.remediation: Implement a WebViewClient that overrides shouldOverrideUrlLoading to restrict allowed hosts, or use custom URL schemes instead of JavaScript interfaces.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. User opens the WebView loading local asset.
2. Attacker induces navigation to a malicious remote page (e.g., open redirect or user click).
3. Malicious page uses window.WebAppInterface to invoke native methods and perform unauthorized actions.

rules.title: Cross-origin dialog hijacking via unvalidated onJsAlert message
rules.description: The onJsAlert handler displays the attacker-controlled `message` in a native dialog without validating that the `url` parameter belongs to a trusted origin, allowing untrusted web content to phish the user or misrepresent app dialogs.
rules.remediation: Validate that the `url` parameter matches an expected origin before displaying the message, or silence the alert entirely for untrusted hosts.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Attacker injects or loads a malicious page in the WebView (e.g., via intent URL or XSS).
2. The page triggers `alert('Fake system dialog requests your password')`.
3. The app shows a native AlertDialog with that message, appearing to come from the app itself.

rules.title: Missing URL validation in onJsAlert allows phishing
rules.description: The onJsAlert handler displays unsanitized JavaScript alert messages without verifying the URL of the originating page, allowing a malicious web page to display arbitrary messages that may trick users.
rules.remediation: Validate the URL before displaying the alert and either block alerts from untrusted origins or display the origin in the dialog.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Load a malicious web page that calls alert('Fake system message...').
2. The native dialog shows the message without indicating the origin.
3. User may be tricked into believing the dialog is from the app or system.

rules.title: Command Injection via Shell Execution of User-Supplied Parameter
rules.description: The method passes the unsanitized parameter 'time' directly into a shell command executed via Runtime.exec, allowing arbitrary command execution.
rules.remediation: Avoid using shell execution. If absolutely necessary, escape or whitelist the input, or use a safe API that does not involve command line parsing.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call getTime with a string like '; reboot'
2. The injected command is executed by the shell
3. Arbitrary commands run with the app's privileges

rules.title: Command Injection via JavaScript Interface getTime method
rules.description: The getTime JavaScript interface method passes the 'Time' parameter directly to Runtime.getRuntime().exec() without sanitization, allowing arbitrary shell command execution from WebView.
rules.remediation: Do not expose shell execution to JavaScript; if necessary, use a whitelist of allowed commands and avoid passing user input to exec.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Load the WebView in the app
2. Inject JavaScript call: AndroidBridge.getTime('some; malicious; command')
3. The command executes with app privileges

rules.title: Arbitrary URL Loading via loadWebsite JavaScript Interface leading to XSS
rules.description: The loadWebsite JavaScript interface method loads any URL passed from JavaScript without validation, allowing an attacker to load javascript: URLs and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the WebView context.
rules.remediation: Validate the URL scheme and host against a whitelist, or avoid exposing loadUrl directly to JavaScript.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Invoke AndroidBridge.loadWebsite('javascript:alert(document.cookie)')
2. The JavaScript executes in the origin of the loaded page

rules.title: JavaScript Interface Exposed to Untrusted Content via Deep Link
rules.description: The WebView loads content from a deep link (potentially attacker-controlled) while having JavaScript enabled and an exposed JavaScript interface ('AndroidBridge'), allowing malicious pages to invoke native Java methods and potentially achieve remote code execution.
rules.remediation: Remove the JavaScript interface if not strictly necessary, or restrict deep link handling to only load trusted local assets. Validate all deep link URLs and ensure only approved origins can interact with the interface.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Craft an intent with a malicious URL (e.g., http://attacker.com/exploit) that triggers this activity via deep link.
2. The WebView loads attacker's page, which contains JavaScript accessing 'AndroidBridge' to call exposed Java methods.
3. Attacker executes arbitrary Java code or accesses sensitive device features.

rules.title: Arbitrary URL loading via @JavascriptInterface without validation
rules.description: The method loadWebsite exposed to JavaScript through @JavascriptInterface passes the user-controlled URL directly to webView.loadUrl() without any validation, allowing an attacker to load arbitrary web content or local files.
rules.remediation: Validate the URL scheme (allow only http/https), implement a domain whitelist, and consider overriding shouldOverrideUrlLoading to restrict navigation.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Attacker gains ability to execute JavaScript in the WebView (e.g., via content injection or a compromised page).
2. Calls loadWebsite('http://attacker.com/phishing') or loadWebsite('file:///data/data/com.example/shared_prefs/...').
3. The WebView loads the attacker-chosen URL, potentially displaying a phishing page or leaking local file content.

rules.title: Command Injection via unsanitized exec parameter
rules.description: The function getTime takes a user-supplied string and passes it directly to Runtime.exec(), allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands.
rules.remediation: Do not pass user input to Runtime.exec(). Use a parameterized API or whitelist allowable commands. If exec must be used, sanitize input by removing shell metacharacters.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Provide a malicious input like '; rm -rf /' as the Time parameter.
2. The command executes with the application's privileges.

rules.title: Plaintext password comparison indicates insecure credential storage
rules.description: LoginActivity compares the entered password directly with the stored value via Intrinsics.areEqual(user.getPassword(), inputPassword), showing passwords are stored without hashing. An attacker who obtains the SQLite database can recover all accounts' credentials.
rules.remediation: Do not store passwords in plaintext; store salted hashes (e.g., BCrypt/Argon2) and verify the input by hashing with the same salt/algorithm.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Obtain the app's SQLite database via backup or root access.
2. Query the users table and read the stored password column.
3. Use the plaintext password to log in as the target user.

rules.title: SQL injection in addUser via unsanitized username
rules.description: The username is concatenated directly into the INSERT statement without parameterization, allowing an attacker-controlled username to alter the SQL query and potentially modify or extract data.
rules.remediation: Use SQLiteDatabase.insert() with ContentValues or execSQL() with bind arguments instead of string concatenation.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Enter a username such as x', 'x', 'x', 1)-- in the registration/login form.
2. Observe that the raw SQL is constructed with the payload inserted verbatim.
3. The injected SQL can modify the INSERT, bypass logic, or enable further SQL injection attacks.

rules.title: User password stored with reversible Base64 encoding
rules.description: Passwords are encoded with Base64 before being stored in SQLite, which is not encryption and can be trivially reversed if the database is extracted.
rules.remediation: Store passwords using a salted, computationally expensive hash such as PBKDF2, bcrypt, or scrypt. Never store reversible password material.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Obtain the app database file (e.g. /data/data/com.mobilehackinglab.foodstore/databases/userdatabase.db).
2. Read the password column from the users table.
3. Base64-decode the stored value to recover the plaintext password.

rules.title: SQL injection in addUser via string concatenation
rules.description: The username is concatenated directly into an INSERT SQL statement without parameterization, allowing a malicious username to alter the query, inject additional SQL, or corrupt the database. Password and address are Base64-encoded but the username is raw user input.
rules.remediation: Use parameterized statements or SQLiteDatabase.insert() with ContentValues instead of building SQL by string concatenation.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Open the app and navigate to the user registration/creation form.
2. Enter a username containing SQL metacharacters, e.g. x', 'y', 'z'); DROP TABLE users; --
3. Submit the form and observe the injected SQL executes, causing data loss or unauthorized modification.

rules.title: Password and address stored as reversible Base64 in SQLite
rules.description: The user password and address are stored inside the SQLite database using Base64 encoding, which is trivially reversible and does not provide real confidentiality or integrity protection. Any attacker able to read the database file can recover plaintext credentials and personal data.
rules.remediation: Encrypt sensitive columns with AES-GCM using a key from the Android Keystore, or use SQLCipher for database encryption. Passwords should be stored as salted hashes (e.g., BCrypt), not reversible Base64 values.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Obtain the app's SQLite database (e.g., /data/data/<package>/databases/users.db).
2. Open the users table and extract the password and address columns.
3. Decode the Base64 values using `base64 -d` or an online decoder to recover plaintext data.

rules.title: User password stored in plaintext via DBHelper
rules.description: The signup flow passes the raw user-supplied password directly to DBHelper.addUser without hashing or encryption, resulting in plaintext credential storage in the app's SQLite database.
rules.remediation: Hash passwords with a strong adaptive one-way algorithm such as BCrypt or Argon2 before storing them; never store plaintext or reversible credentials in SQLite.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Launch the app and register a new user with a known password.
2. Root the device/emulator and copy the app database from /data/data/com.mobilehackinglab.foodstore/databases/.
3. Open the database with sqlite3 and inspect the users table to observe the plaintext password.

rules.title: Client-side credit balance check can be bypassed
rules.description: Order checkout validates and deducts user credits entirely in the client process. An attacker can tamper with the value of userCredit or instrument the method with Frida/repackaging to bypass payment for any order.
rules.remediation: Move credit validation and deduction to a trusted backend API and never rely on client-side balances or success flags. Tamper-proof the price and order data with signatures.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Launch the app and choose an expensive item.
2. Attempt to order it and observe the 'Insufficient credits' toast.
3. Use Frida or a memory editor to set userCredit to a high value before the click handler runs.
4. Order the item again and observe that the order succeeds with no server-side credit validation.

rules.title: Sensitive password field exposed in toString()
rules.description: The User.toString() method appends the password field to the returned string. If the object is logged, printed, or included in an exception message, the plaintext password may be exposed to logs or other system output channels.
rules.remediation: Remove the password field from toString(), or mask it (e.g., "password=***"). Never include credentials in object string representations or log messages.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Any code path that invokes Log.d(...) or String.valueOf(user) on a User instance triggers toString().
2. The returned string contains the plaintext password.
3. The password is written to the Android log or included in a serialized/displayed string, exposing it to local attackers or log aggregation.

rules.title: Plaintext password comparison in login auth logic
rules.description: The login flow compares the user-supplied plaintext password directly with the stored password field, indicating that user passwords are stored without hashing and can be exposed if the database is compromised.
rules.remediation: Store only a salted password hash (e.g., BCrypt) and verify the password using a dedicated password hashing API instead of comparing the raw stored value.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Obtain a database dump through backup, root access, or another vulnerability.
2. Read the plaintext password value from the users table.
3. Use the leaked credentials to log in as any user.

rules.title: SQL injection in addUser via unsanitized username
rules.description: The addUser method concatenates the User-supplied username directly into an INSERT statement, allowing an attacker to manipulate the SQL query.
rules.remediation: Use SQLiteDatabase.insert or a parameterized query with ? placeholders instead of string concatenation.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger addUser with a User whose username is: '); DROP TABLE users;--
2. Observe the users table is deleted
3. Or use: admin'-- to inject arbitrary data

rules.title: User passwords stored with reversible Base64 encoding in SQLite
rules.description: Passwords are encoded with Base64 before being persisted, which is not encryption and can be trivially decoded if the database is exposed through backup or device compromise.
rules.remediation: Store only a salted hash of the password (e.g. BCrypt/PBKDF2) and avoid reversible encoding for credentials.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Register a user via addUser
2. Open userdatabase.db from app data or backup
3. Decode the password column from Base64 to recover the plaintext password

rules.title: Unsanitized fileName enables path traversal when copying assets
rules.description: The fileName parameter is used directly as the output file name in new File(CopyUtil.DOWNLOADS_DIRECTORY, fileName), allowing a caller to provide paths such as ../../ to write outside the intended directory.
rules.remediation: Validate and sanitize fileName: reject any path containing ".." or absolute path segments, and verify the canonical output path starts with DOWNLOADS_DIRECTORY's canonical path before writing.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call copyFileFromAssets(context, "../../evil.txt")
2. The coroutine creates a File in the downloads directory resolving to a path outside it.
3. The asset is copied to the traversed location if the parent directories exist or are created.
4. This can overwrite or create arbitrary files within application-readable storage.

rules.title: SQL injection in addUser via unescaped username
rules.description: The username is concatenated directly into an INSERT SQL statement and executed with execSQL, allowing an attacker to manipulate the query by injecting SQL fragments through the username field.
rules.remediation: Use parameterized queries (SQLiteStatement or ContentValues) instead of string concatenation when inserting user data.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create a User object with username: '); DROP TABLE users; --
2. Pass the object to addUser()
3. The crafted username is concatenated into the SQL statement and executed, potentially dropping the table or extracting data

rules.title: Password stored using reversible Base64 encoding instead of hashing
rules.description: The user password is Base64-encoded and stored in a local SQLite database. Base64 is not an encryption or hash function, so anyone with access to the database can trivially recover the plaintext password.
rules.remediation: Store only a salted password hash (e.g., PBKDF2 or bcrypt) and never store the password in plaintext or reversible encoding.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call addUser() with a known password
2. Inspect the SQLite database file (e.g., via backup or rooted device)
3. Decode the stored Base64 string to recover the password

rules.title: Path traversal in copyFileFromUri via untrusted Uri last path segment
rules.description: The last path segment from the user-controlled Uri is used unsanitized in a File constructor, allowing encoded traversal sequences to escape the intended DOWNLOADS_DIRECTORY and write/overwrite arbitrary files in the app's writable storage.
rules.remediation: Validate and sanitize the file name before constructing the output File: reject path separators, absolute paths, and traversal sequences such as '..' or '%2e%2e', or use Files.createTempFile / a safe basename extraction.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Supply a content/file Uri whose last path segment contains encoded traversal, e.g. ..%2F..%2Fvictim.txt
2. Invoke copyFileFromUri(uri)
3. Observe the output file being created outside DOWNLOADS_DIRECTORY, potentially overwriting another file

rules.title: Password stored as reversible Base64 in SQLite database
rules.description: The getUserByUsername method decodes passwords that were stored as Base64, indicating credentials are persisted in a reversible format instead of being hashed. An attacker with access to the database file can recover plaintext passwords trivially.
rules.remediation: Store passwords using a strong one-way hash with a unique salt (e.g., bcrypt, PBKDF2, or Argon2). Never use reversible encoding such as Base64 for credential storage.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Obtain the app's SQLite database file from the device (e.g., /data/data/com.mobilehackinglab.foodstore/databases/).
2. Open the users table and read the password column.
3. Decode each value using Base64 to recover the plaintext password.

rules.title: User password stored in plaintext via DBHelper.addUser
rules.description: The signup handler reads the password as raw text and passes it directly to DBHelper.addUser in a User object with no hashing or encryption, leaving credentials recoverable from the app's database.
rules.remediation: Hash the password with a strong salted one-way function (e.g. BCrypt/scrypt/Argon2) before constructing the User object and persisting it.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Register a new account in the app.
2. Dump the app database from /data/data/com.mobilehackinglab.foodstore/databases/.
3. Observe the plaintext password in the users table.

rules.title: Plaintext password passed for storage in signup flow
rules.description: The signup callback takes the user-supplied password as plaintext and passes it unencrypted via User to DBHelper.addUser, so the password is likely persisted in cleartext in the app SQLite database.
rules.remediation: Hash the password with a strong salted one-way algorithm (bcrypt/scrypt/PBKDF2) before creating or storing the User, and never store raw password values.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Launch the app and register with a known password.
2. Submit the signup form.
3. Inspect the app's SQLite database (e.g. /data/data/com.mobilehackinglab.foodstore/databases) and observe the password stored as cleartext.

rules.title: Arbitrary local file read via file:// URL scheme
rules.description: The code explicitly opens file:// URLs and copies their contents, allowing a crafted URI to read arbitrary files from the device outside the intended directory.
rules.remediation: Restrict source URIs to content:// and access them via ContentResolver with permission checks, or verify the canonical path is within an allowed directory before opening.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Provide a file:///data/data/com.app/databases/db URL to copyFileFromUri.
2. The function opens the file and writes it to outFile.
3. Sensitive file contents are exposed via LiveData or further processing.

rules.title: Cleartext HTTP used for file downloads
rules.description: Any non-file URL is connected using HttpURLConnection without enforcing HTTPS, subjecting downloaded content to man-in-the-middle interception or modification.
rules.remediation: Refuse non-https URLs and use a network security config that blocks cleartext traffic, or use HTTPS with certificate pinning if the app handles sensitive data.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Supply an http:// URL to copyFileFromUri.
2. The app connects over unencrypted HTTP.
3. A network attacker intercepts or tampers with the downloaded file.

rules.title: Unsanitized fileName enables path traversal when copying assets
rules.description: The copyFileFromAssets method constructs a destination File directly from the fileName parameter without sanitization, allowing '../' sequences to write asset content outside the intended Downloads directory if the fileName is attacker-controlled.
rules.remediation: Validate the fileName by checking its canonical path starts with the intended directory and reject any path containing '..' or path separators.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Supply fileName as '../../evil.txt' to copyFileFromAssets.
2. The method creates a File resolving to the parent of DOWNLOADS_DIRECTORY.
3. Asset content is written to '../../evil.txt', overwriting arbitrary writable files.

rules.title: Arbitrary file read via file:// URL in copyFileFromUri
rules.description: The copyFileFromUri coroutine accepts a caller-controlled URL and, if its protocol is file://, reads the referenced local file and copies it to an output file exposed via LiveData. A malicious intent URI can force the app to copy any file it can read (e.g. shared preferences, databases) into a location accessible to other components/apps.
rules.remediation: Only allow trusted content:// URIs or explicit user-approved file paths, and reject file:// and other risky URL schemes entirely. Validate that the resolved path stays within the intended app storage directory.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger the document viewer with a file:// URI pointing to an app-readable sensitive file, e.g. file:///data/data/com.mobilehackinglab.documentviewer/shared_prefs/app.xml
2. The app executes copyFileFromUri and opens the file via URL.openStream().
3. The attacker retrieves the copied file from the LiveData-published output URI.

rules.title: Cleartext HTTP download without scheme enforcement
rules.description: When the URL protocol is not file://, the function opens it with HttpURLConnection without checking that the protocol is https://, enabling man-in-the-middle interception or modification of downloaded documents if the app permits cleartext traffic.
rules.remediation: Enforce https:// for all remote URLs, reject http:// schemes at the entry point, and configure Network Security Policy or certificate pinning to prevent cleartext and MITM.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Supply an http:// URL (e.g. http://attacker.example/malicious.pdf) as the document URI.
2. The app invokes copyFileFromUri and downloads over plaintext HTTP.
3. An on-path attacker intercepts or replaces the document content before it is saved and shared.

rules.title: Command Injection via unsanitized shell command
rules.description: The message parameter is concatenated into a /bin/sh -c command without sanitization, allowing arbitrary shell command execution if the message is attacker-controlled.
rules.remediation: Avoid using /bin/sh -c; invoke the script directly with ProcessBuilder and pass message as a separate argument, or strictly validate/escape all message content.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call runCowsay with message containing shell metacharacters, e.g. "hello; id"
2. Observe that /bin/sh executes the injected command
3. The command output or side effects are returned or visible

rules.title: JavaScript injection in WebView via Base64 deep-link message
rules.description: A crafted VIEW intent supplies a Base64 URL-encoded path that is decoded and concatenated directly into a javascript: URL loaded by the WebView. Only single quotes are escaped, so backslashes and other metacharacters can break out of the string and execute arbitrary JavaScript with access to the WebAppInterface bridge.
rules.remediation: Never concatenate untrusted values into javascript: URLs. Use WebView.evaluateJavascript with JSON.stringify for the argument or a safe origin-checked postMessage channel, and validate the intent's source.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Encode payload like \');alert(1);// using Base64 URL-safe alphabet.
2. Start intent: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d 'postboard://postmessage/<encoded_payload>'
3. The activity decodes and evaluates the injected JavaScript.
4. JS can call every @JavascriptInterface method exposed by WebAppInterface.

rules.title: WebView JavaScript bridge exposed with addJavascriptInterface
rules.description: JavaScript is enabled and a native WebAppInterface object is exposed to JavaScript via addJavascriptInterface. Any page loaded in this WebView, or any XSS within the local HTML, can invoke Java methods exposed by the interface, potentially leading to code execution or data leakage depending on the exposed methods and Android version.
rules.remediation: Remove addJavascriptInterface unless strictly necessary, and only enable JavaScript for fully trusted content. When a bridge is required, expose only safe, input-validated methods and restrict WebView navigation to trusted URLs.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Load attacker-controlled or untrusted content into the WebView, or trigger an XSS in the loaded HTML.
2. Execute JavaScript in the WebView to call exposed WebAppInterface methods, reaching native functionality with the app's privileges.

rules.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized markdown in WebAppInterface
rules.description: postMarkdownMessage converts user-supplied markdown into HTML without sanitizing raw HTML or validating URL schemes, so an attacker can inject scripts or javascript: links that execute when the message is rendered in a WebView.
rules.remediation: Sanitize all generated HTML with an allowlist-based sanitizer and reject javascript:, data:, and other dangerous URL schemes before storing or rendering messages.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call postMarkdownMessage through the exposed JavascriptInterface with payload: <script>alert(1)</script> or [x](javascript:alert(1)).
2. The crafted message is stored by cache.addMessage().
3. When getMessages() is rendered in the WebView, the payload executes as stored XSS.
